claim.pdf_says: Under "Fractional-seconds time formats": "Basic local time      hhmmss.sssss      051427.8124" (five "s" characters after the period; verified by cropping and enlarging the printed row — every other row on the page has four).
claim.why_it_matters: The transcription silently normalises the printed token from five "s" to four. It is almost certainly an ISO typographical defect (page 1198 states "four \"s\" characters after the period are used for illustrative purposes", and the paired value 051427.8124 has four fractional digits), but the reconciled markdown is supposed to BE the printed page; quietly repairing a printed defect makes the defect invisible to anyone using this file as the citable source, and makes any future PDF-vs-markdown diff report a phantom mismatch here.

verdict.reasoning: CONFIRMED by two independent methods, and I tried hard to refute it. (1) PIXELS: rendered spec_p1197.png at 300 dpi (printed folio 1167) and ran a column ink-cluster analysis over the Formats column of all six Fractional-seconds rows. The 'Basic local time' row yields, after the period cluster at x=178-182, FIVE separate glyph clusters (187-201, 206-221, 226-240, 244-259, 264-278), each 14-15 px wide — the 's' advance. Every sibling row yields four: 'Basic UTC time' has four s then a 20 px 'Z' at 264-284; 'Basic offset time' has four s then a 19 px '+' at 264-283. A 6x tight crop of the token reads 'hhmmss.sssss' unambiguously; the matching crop of the UTC row reads 'hhmmss.ssssZ'. So the fifth glyph is not a smudge, a wide 's', or a mis-segmented 'Z'/'+'. (2) TEXT LAYER: the PDF content stream is an obfuscated shift cipher (lowercase 'a'=U+0083, digits at U+0372+n, '.'=U+01E4, ':'=U+01E3, '+'=U+03AA; uppercase is dropped by extraction, which is why the 'Z' and the 'B' of 'Basic' do not appear). Decoding the six Formats cells on PDF page index 1196 gives: hhmmss.sssss (len 12), hh:mm:ss.ssss, hhmmss.ssss(Z), hh:mm:ss.ssss(Z), hhmmss.ssss+hhmm, hh:mm:ss.ssdd+hh:mm. The first cell is literally twelve characters with five 's' in the PDF's own character stream — this is NOT a render or OCR artifact. (3) MARKDOWN: specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 48368 reads '| Basic local time | hhmmss.ssss | 051427.8124 |' — four 's'. The claim quotes both sources accurately. The divergence is one character, it is real, and it is not reflow, wrapping, hyphenation, or page-break furniture. REFUTATION ATTEMPTS THAT FAILED: (a) 'the fifth s is really the Z/plus of the next token' — no, the Basic local row has no trailing Z or '+', and the extra cluster is 14 px (s-width), not 19-20 px; (b) 'the markdown just reflowed it' — no, it is a table cell, character-for-character comparable; (c) 'the transcription deliberately normalises printed defects' — refuted from inside the same table: line 48373 faithfully preserves the sibling ISO typo 'hh:mm:ss.ssdd+hh:mm' (the printed 'dd' is in the PDF text layer too). The transcription therefore preserves one printed defect in this table and silently repairs another, which is exactly the inconsistency the claim describes.
verdict.corrected_description: REAL, with two refinements to the wording. (1) The printed page (folio 1167 / PDF page 1197) sets the Fractional-seconds 'Basic local time' Formats cell as 'hhmmss.sssss' — five 's' after the period — confirmed both by 300 dpi glyph-cluster measurement AND by decoding the PDF's own obfuscated text layer, which carries a 12-character token h,h,m,m,s,s,.,s,s,s,s,s. It is not an artifact of rendering or of the OCR pass. specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 48368 transcribes it as 'hhmmss.ssss' (four). (2) The claim's aside that 'every other row on the page has four' should read 'every other fractional row prints four fractional-second placeholder characters' — the Extended offset time row prints 'hh:mm:ss.ssdd+hh:mm' (two 's' then two 'd'), itself an ISO typographical defect, and the markdown DOES reproduce that one verbatim at line 48373. That contrast is the strongest evidence for the finding: within a single six-row table the transcription preserves one printed defect and silently repairs another, so no consistent editorial normalisation policy explains it. Severity 'cosmetic' is correct: Annex D.31.5.2 is informative, the formats are explicitly illustrative, and page 1198 (line 48385) notes the number of 's' after the decimal separator may range from 1 to 9, so 'hhmmss.sssss' denotes a legal format either way — no normative behavior is affected. The fix is to restore the printed five 's' at line 48368 and annotate it as an ISO defect (cross-referencing line 48341 on this same page and line 48385 on page 1198, both of which use four), rather than to leave the page silently repaired.
